paper_metadata.title: Portfolio Optimization Based on Quantum HHL Algorithm

summary: The paper presents a 3-asset portfolio optimization problem encoded as a constrained quadratic program and converted to a linear system solved with HHL. The reported quantum setup uses 9 qubits, 2 phase-estimation bits, and a success-probability estimate of 0.9, producing an approximate normalized solution (0.1608, 0.2557, 0.5833) that is close to the exact classical solution (0.16216216, 0.25675676, 0.58108108).

experiments.description: Portfolio optimization formulated as a quadratic programming problem with equality constraints and solved using the HHL linear-systems algorithm on IBM Qiskit hardware/simulation.

algorithm.variant: HHL algorithm for portfolio optimization / quadratic programming with equality constraints

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Portfolio weights are encoded by transforming the constrained quadratic program into a linear system A|x>=|b>; the input vector b is expanded to 8 dimensions so that 3 qubits can represent it, and A is expanded to 8x8 for the quantum linear-systems routine.
problem_formulation.objective_function: min_w w^T Σ w subject to μ^T w = μ0 and P^T w = ξ
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Equality constraints handled via Lagrange multipliers and conversion to a linear system; solution extracted by post-selecting the ancilla measurement result 1.

problem_instance.description: Three-asset portfolio optimization example with specified mean returns and correlation matrix.
problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Set P=(1,1,1)^T; expand b to 8 dimensions with zero padding; expand A to 8x8; use 2-bit phase estimation and 0.9 success probability estimate.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Compare normalized approximate solution from HHL with exact classical solution; report component ratios and normalized vector.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Formulate portfolio optimization as a constrained quadratic program; convert to linear system using Lagrange multipliers; pad to 8-dimensional input.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Measure ancilla qubit; when ancilla=1, read the register corresponding to portfolio weights; normalize amplitudes to obtain investment proportions.

speedup_claims.conditions: Under the standard HHL assumptions for solving linear systems
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states exponential acceleration in general for HHL, but does not provide an empirical runtime comparison for this portfolio instance.

speedup_claims.conditions: under HHL assumptions for solving linear systems
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the linear-systems problem is transformed into a quantum problem and solved with HHL; no empirical runtime comparison is reported.
The paper states exponential acceleration for linear systems under HHL assumptions, but does not provide an empirical runtime comparison or hardware-scale demonstration.

speedup_claims.conditions: under HHL assumptions for solving linear systems

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Exponential acceleration for linear systems under HHL assumptions

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: The paper uses a 3-asset toy portfolio instance, expands b to 8 dimensions, and states the full HHL circuit requires 9 qubits; no scaling study or hardware benchmark is provided.
limiting_factors: Only a toy 3-asset example is solved
No runtime, gate count, or hardware noise data are reported
Comparison is only against the exact classical solution for the same small instance
HHL is presented as a feasibility demonstration rather than a practical speedup

notes: Hardware is reported only as implementation with Qiskit on IBM's quantum computing platform; no specific device or simulator is named, so hardware.type is left not_specified.
9 qubits is inferred from the paper's statement that the whole HHL circuit requires 9 qubits.
Circuit depth is not explicitly reported; only the phase-estimation bit count and qubit count are given.
The paper claims the approximate solution is close to the exact solution, but does not demonstrate practical quantum advantage.

Reported values include 9 qubits total, 2 estimated phase-estimation bits, success probability estimate 0.9, and normalized approximate solution (0.1608, 0.2557, 0.5833) versus exact (0.16216216, 0.25675676, 0.58108108).
